disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 8.4% falls in the diabetes range, which means your blood sugar has been running higher than what is considered healthy. Your main risk factors are low physical activity, being over 45, and having an existing kidney condition that needs extra attention. The most valuable next steps are getting your kidney function, blood pressure, and vitamin B12 checked, staying consistent with gentle regular activity, and following the protein and potassium guidance in your food plan. Your BMI is in the normal range, which is a helpful starting point for building healthier habits.

comorbidity_assessment.note: Kidneys help filter excess sugar and waste from the blood, so when blood sugar stays high for a long time it can add extra strain on kidney function. Because of this, keeping an eye on kidney tests and following protein and potassium guidance is especially important for you.

constraints: Do not follow high-protein diets or take protein supplements; keep protein moderate unless your kidney doctor advises otherwise.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; ask your doctor whether you need to limit potassium or phosphorus.

foods_to_eat: Low-potassium vegetables like cabbage, cauliflower, green beans, and bottle gourd
Whole grains such as broken wheat, millets, and small portions of rice
Moderate plant protein sources like tofu and soy milk in small amounts
High-fibre foods like oats and whole grain rotis
Fresh fruits in small portions such as apple and papaya, chosen for lower potassium content
Herbs and spices like cumin, coriander, turmeric, and curry leaves for flavour without salt
foods_to_avoid: Deep-fried snacks like pakoras and samosas
Refined flour products such as white bread and maida-based items
High-potassium foods like bananas, oranges, potatoes, and tomatoes in large amounts unless advised otherwise
High-protein plant foods in large portions, such as large servings of lentils or soy products
plan.portion_guidance: Keep meals moderate in size using small bowls and katoris. Focus on vegetables and whole grains, and keep protein-rich foods like soy and lentils to small portions as part of a kidney-friendly, moderate protein approach. Avoid large servings of any single food group.
plan.hydration: Drink water through the day as guided by your routine, and discuss with your doctor how much fluid is right for you given your kidney health.
based_on: kidney disease: moderate protein, avoid potassium-based salt substitutes

exercise: Start with gentle seated or standing exercises for 10 minutes a day, such as chair yoga or stretching, and slowly build up as your comfort allows.

Aim to work up gradually toward 150 minutes a week of moderate activity like walking or light cycling, plus simple strengthening movements (such as using light resistance bands or bodyweight exercises) on 2 days a week.
Because kidney disease can affect energy and fluid balance, check with your healthcare team before increasing activity intensity, and stop if you feel dizzy, breathless, or very tired.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk, 5 days a week, at a comfortable pace. Gradually build up by a few minutes every week until you reach about 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your body allows.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the normal range, so the focus is on maintaining your current weight rather than losing weight. Keep eating a balanced vegan diet with steady meal timing and stay physically active to support your overall health.
lifestyle.sleep: Try to get 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, quiet, and dark to help you fall asleep more easily.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5 to 10 minutes a day to help calm your mind and body.
Try gentle mindfulness or meditation practices, such as guided relaxation apps or quiet reflection, a few times a week.
Spend time on enjoyable, low-pressure activities like listening to music, gardening, or connecting with family to help manage daily stress.
behaviour_change: Avoid using painkillers such as ibuprofen regularly without checking with your doctor first, since these can affect kidney health.
Keep track of your HbA1c and kidney function with regular check-ups so you and your healthcare team can monitor your progress together.
Since you don't smoke or drink, keep up these healthy habits as they support both your heart and kidney health.
based_on: Constraint: avoid regular painkiller use without medical advice

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

preventive_actions: Schedule kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio testing, along with blood pressure and vitamin B12 checks.
Add light daily movement, such as short walks, to counter a sedentary routine.
Keep protein intake moderate and avoid protein supplements unless your kidney doctor says otherwise.
Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and ask your doctor about potassium or phosphorus limits.
Avoid regular use of over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen without medical advice.
Follow your 1600 calorie target and plan vegan meals that fit your protein and potassium guidance.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
